title: What is Recursion
summary: Defines recursion as defining an object, mathematical function, or computer function in terms of itself, with GNU as a real-world example.
main_text: Recursion is defining an object, mathematical function, or computer function in terms of itself. A well-known real-world example is GNU (makers of gedit, g++ compiler, etc.), where GNU stands for 'GNU is Not Unix.' This is a recursive acronym because the definition of GNU contains GNU itself, leading to an infinite expansion: GNU is Not Unix is not Unix is Not Unix... The concept is also illustrated by Russian nesting dolls (matryoshka), where each doll contains a smaller version of itself, visually representing the self-referential nature of recursion.
notes_text: The GNU acronym is a classic example of recursion in naming conventions in computer science. The matryoshka dolls analogy helps visualize how recursive structures contain smaller copies of themselves. Unlike the GNU acronym which recurses infinitely, practical recursive functions must have a stopping condition (base case).

images.description: Russian nesting dolls (matryoshka) showing progressively smaller dolls to illustrate the concept of self-similar recursive structures
Tree diagram showing the recursive expansion of GNU = GNU is Not Unix, with each occurrence of GNU expanding again into 'GNU is Not Unix'

title: Recursion: Base Case and Recursive Case
summary: Explains recursion as solving problems using smaller versions of itself with a base/terminating case, using factorial as the primary example.
main_text: Recursion is a problem in which the solution can be expressed in terms of smaller versions of itself and a base/terminating case. It can often take the place of a loop OR lead to much more elegant coding solutions compared to using a loop. Input (arguments) to the problem should be categorized as a: Base case: Small version of problem whose known beforehand or easily computable (no recursion needed). Recursive case: Solution can be described using solutions to smaller problems of the same type. Keeping putting in terms of something smaller until we reach the base case. Factorial example: n! = n * (n-1) * (n-2) * ... * 2 * 1. This can be rewritten as n! = n * (n-1)!. Base case: n = 1. Recursive case: n > 1 => n*(n-1)!
notes_text: The factorial function is the canonical introductory example of recursion. The key insight is recognizing that n! can be defined in terms of (n-1)!, which is a smaller instance of the same problem. Every recursive solution must have both a base case (stopping condition) and a recursive case (the self-referential step that reduces the problem size).

title: Recursive Function Mechanics
summary: Shows the general outline for writing recursive functions in C code, emphasizing base case first, recurse on smaller problems, and separate memory per instance.
main_text: General outline for recursive functions: Put the base case check first. Ensure you recurse on a smaller problem (e.g. f(n) should NOT recurse on f(n) but a smaller version of the problem like f(n-1)). This structure will help avoid infinite recursions. C Code example for factorial: int fact(int n) { if(n == 1) { // base case return 1; } else { // recursive case return n * fact(n-1); } }. While the code is shared by each running instance of the function, the system stack provides separate areas of memory for each instance of a recursive function. Thus, each local variable and actual parameter of a function is separate and isolated from other recursive function instances (e.g. each fact(n) has its own version of n).
notes_text: The structure of checking the base case first is a best practice that prevents accidental infinite recursion. The key mechanical insight is that although there is only one copy of the function code in memory, each call gets its own stack frame with its own copy of local variables and parameters. This is what makes recursion possible at the hardware level.

title: Recursion and the Stack
summary: Demonstrates how the system stack stores separate memory frames for each recursive call, using factorial(4) with memory addresses and return links.
main_text: Must return back through EACH call. The slide shows the Stack Area of RAM for computing fact(4). Each recursive call creates a new stack frame with its own copy of parameter n and a return link. Starting from main() which has val=4 at address 0xbf8, fact(4) is called creating a frame at 0xbf0 with n=4, then fact(3) at 0xbe8 with n=3, fact(2) at 0xbe0 with n=2, and fact(1) at 0xbd8 with n=1. Each frame stores the return link (004001844 pointing to line L9 for recursive calls, or 004001844 pointing to L16 for the initial call from main). The return values propagate back: fact(1) returns 1, fact(2) returns 2, fact(3) returns 6, fact(4) returns 24. Value/version of n is implicitly 'saved' and 'restored' as we move from one instance of the fact function to the next.
notes_text: This slide is critical for understanding the mechanics of recursion at the memory level. Each stack frame is independent, which is why each instance of fact() can have a different value of n. The return link tells the CPU where to resume execution after each recursive call returns. The stack grows downward in memory (from higher to lower addresses) with each new function call.

images.description: Diagram showing the system stack with 5 stack frames (main, fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), fact(1)) stacked vertically. Each frame shows memory addresses, the value of n, and return link addresses. Arrows show the chain of calls and returns with computed values 1, 2, 6, 24.

title: Recursive Analysis Tip: Box Diagrams
summary: Introduces box diagrams as a tool for analyzing recursive functions, showing one box per function instance with arguments, local variables, and return values.
main_text: To analyze recursive functions draw a box diagram which is a simplified view of each function instance on the stack. One box per function. Show arguments, pertinent local variables, and return values. Show line number of indicator for where the previous call paused (and where it should resume upon return). Example uses a modified factorial with temporary variable t: int fact(int n) { if(n == 1) { return 1; } else { int t = fact(n-1); return n * t; } }. The box diagram for fact(4) shows: Main() calls fact(4) which pauses at L07, fact(4) has n=4, t=6, returns 4*6=24. fact(3) has n=3, t=2, returns 2*3=6. fact(2) has n=2, t=1, returns 1*2=2. fact(1) has n=1, returns 1.
notes_text: Box diagrams are an essential study and debugging tool for understanding recursive execution. They visually show the chain of calls and returns, making it easier to trace through recursive logic. The line number indicator (L07) shows where execution pauses when a recursive call is made, which is where it will resume when that call returns.

images.description: Box diagram showing four boxes connected by arrows representing fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), and fact(1). Each box contains n and t values. Arrows show L07 pause points between calls, and return values flowing back: 1, 1*2=2, 2*3=6, 4*6=24.

title: Work Before Or After Recursion
summary: Presents two code snippets for doit(3) to illustrate how placing work before vs. after the recursive call changes output order.
main_text: Predict the output of each of these code snippets for a call to doit(3). Left version (work before recursion): void doit(int n) { if(n == 1) cout << 'Stop'; else { cout << 'Go' << endl; doit(n-1); } }. Right version (work after recursion): void doit(int n) { if(n == 1) cout << 'Stop'; else { doit(n-1); cout << 'Go' << endl; } }. In the left version, 'Go' is printed before the recursive call, so output appears in forward order. In the right version, the recursive call happens first, so output appears in reverse order. This exercise demonstrates the fundamental difference between doing work before versus after the recursive call.
notes_text: This is a critical exercise for understanding recursion execution order. When work is done before the recursive call, it executes in the order of the calls (top-down). When work is done after the recursive call, it executes in reverse order (bottom-up) because the work waits until the recursion returns.

title: Head vs. Tail Recursion Definitions
summary: Defines head recursion (recursive call before work) and tail recursion (work before recursive call), with side-by-side code examples.
main_text: Head Recursion: Recursive call is made before the real work is performed in the function body. Tail Recursion: Some work is performed and then the recursive call is made. Tail Recursion example: void doit(int n) { if(n == 1) cout << 'Stop' << endl; else { cout << 'Go' << endl; doit(n-1); } }. In this version, 'Go' is printed first (the work), then the recursive call doit(n-1) is made. Head Recursion example: void doit(int n) { if(n == 1) cout << 'Stop' << endl; else { doit(n-1); cout << 'Go' << endl; } }. In this version, the recursive call doit(n-1) is made first, then 'Go' is printed after the call returns.
notes_text: Understanding head vs. tail recursion is important for predicting output order and for optimization. Tail recursive functions can sometimes be optimized by compilers into iterative loops (tail call optimization), eliminating stack frame overhead. Head recursion processes results on the way back up from the deepest call, while tail recursion processes on the way down.

title: Head vs. Tail Recursion Output Comparison
summary: Shows the complete execution trace and output of tail recursion (Go, Go, Stop) vs head recursion (Stop, Go, Go) for doit(3).
main_text: Tail Recursion: Some work is performed and then the recursive call is made. Head Recursion: Recursive call is made before the real work is performed in the function body. Tail Recursion trace for doit(3): doit(3) prints 'Go' then calls doit(2), doit(2) prints 'Go' then calls doit(1), doit(1) prints 'Stop'. Output order: Go, Go, Stop. Each function returns after making its recursive call. Head Recursion trace for doit(3): doit(3) calls doit(2) first, doit(2) calls doit(1) first, doit(1) prints 'Stop', then doit(2) prints 'Go' on return, then doit(3) prints 'Go' on return. Output order: Stop, Go, Go. The key difference is that tail recursion outputs in forward order while head recursion outputs in reverse order.
notes_text: The box diagrams on this slide clearly show the difference in execution flow. In tail recursion, work happens on the way DOWN the recursive chain. In head recursion, work happens on the way BACK UP. This is visually represented by the target/bullseye diagrams showing the order of output.

images.description: Two side-by-side execution traces showing tail recursion (left) with doit(3)->doit(2)->doit(1) printing Go,Go,Stop in forward order, and head recursion (right) printing Stop,Go,Go in reverse order. Box diagrams show each function instance with its output and return flow.

title: Exercise: Count-down and Count-up
summary: Exercise slide directing students to practice writing recursive count-down and count-up functions.
main_text: Exercises: Count-down and Count-up. Students are asked to write recursive functions for counting down and counting up. A count-down function would use tail recursion (print current number, then recurse with n-1). A count-up function would use head recursion (recurse with n-1 first, then print current number on the way back up).
notes_text: These exercises reinforce the head vs. tail recursion concepts. Count-down naturally maps to tail recursion (do work first, then recurse), while count-up maps to head recursion (recurse first, then do work on return).

title: Practice: Summing an Array
summary: Introduces the problem of recursively summing an array, showing iterative solution and prompting students to write a recursive version.
main_text: Many loop/iteration-based approaches can be defined recursively as well. How could summing an array be implemented recursively? Goal: Find how 1 or more solutions to smaller problems can be used to produce the solution to the bigger problem. Example array: data[4] = {8, 6, 7, 9} at address 800. Iterative solution (isum): int isum(int data[], int len) { int sum = data[0]; for(int i=1; i < len; i++) { sum += data[i]; } return sum; }. Students are asked to write the recursive version rsum(int data[], int len). The main function calls both: int sum1 = isum(data, size); int sum2 = rsum(data, size);
notes_text: This slide transitions from simple single-value recursion (factorial) to recursion over data structures (arrays). The key insight is identifying what '1 thing' each recursive call is responsible for and how to combine it with the recursive result. For array summing, each call can handle one element and recurse on the remaining elements.

images.description: Array diagram showing data[4] with values {8, 6, 7, 9} at indices 0-3, starting at memory address 800

title: Steps to Formulating Recursive Solutions
summary: Presents two key principles for developing recursive solutions: each call handles one element, then combine that element with the recursive result.
main_text: There are often 2 principles to finding recursive solutions. Principle 1: Usually recursive functions are 'Responsible' for ONLY 1 value / element / item and then use recursion to handle all remaining items. Principle 2: Determine how to combine the 1 element for which you are responsible, and the answer returned by recursion. Assume via the 'magic of recursion' you get the answer for all remaining elements. How can you combine that with your 1 element to form the larger solution? The visual example shows factorial decomposition: a bar represents 4!, which decomposes into one element times 3!, which equals 6, and then 4*6=24.
notes_text: These two principles are the most important takeaway for formulating any recursive solution. Principle 1 identifies the decomposition strategy. Principle 2 identifies the combination strategy. Together they form a complete recursive formulation. The 'magic of recursion' mental model is powerful: trust that the recursive call will give you the correct answer for the smaller problem, and focus only on how to use that answer.

images.description: Visual decomposition showing how a problem (represented as a bar for 4!) is split into one element and a smaller subproblem (3!), with the recursive result (6) combined with the element to produce the final answer (4*6=24)

title: Three Steps to Formulating Recursive Solutions
summary: Outlines three concrete steps: write solutions for sample inputs, identify the base case, and identify how to combine small solutions into larger ones.
main_text: Step 1: Write out some solutions for a few input cases to discover how the problem can be decomposed into smaller problems of the same form. Does solving the problem on an input of smaller value or size help formulate the solution to the larger? Step 2: Identify the base case - an input for which the answer is trivial. Step 3: Identify how to combine the small solution(s) to solve the larger problem. Example with array summing: Len=4: {8,6,7,9} => Answer: 8+6+7+9=30. Len=3: {6,7,9} => Answer: 8+6+7=22 (last 3 elements). Len=3: {8,6,7} => Answer: 8+6+7=21 (first 3 elements). Len=1: {8} => Answer: 8 (base case). The decomposition shows that the sum of 4 elements can be expressed as one element plus the sum of the remaining 3 elements.
notes_text: This three-step process provides a systematic approach to developing recursive solutions. Step 1 is about pattern recognition through concrete examples. Step 2 identifies the stopping condition. Step 3 identifies the recursive relationship. Notice the slide shows two different decomposition strategies: using the last 3 elements or the first 3 elements, demonstrating that there can be multiple valid recursive formulations.

images.description: Multiple array diagrams showing the decomposition of array summing: full array of length 4 with answer 30, subarrays of length 3 with answers 22 and 21, and base case of length 1 with answer 8

title: Recursive Functions: Array Sum Implementation
summary: Applies recursive formulation to array summing, showing the iterative version alongside an incomplete recursive version for students to complete.
main_text: Many loop/iteration-based approaches can be defined recursively as well. How could summing an array be implemented recursively? What 1 thing could each recursion be responsible for? How could we combine that 1 thing with the solution from the recursive call? Once you have a recursive formulation all that's left is the mechanics of the implementation (i.e. arguments and return values). Iterative solution: int isum(int data[], int len) { int sum = data[0]; for(int i=1; i < len; i++) { sum += data[i]; } return sum; }. Recursive solution skeleton: int rsum(int data[], int len) { if(len == 1) return ___; else ___ return ___; }. Students must fill in the blanks for the base case return value and the recursive case.
notes_text: This slide bridges the gap between understanding the recursive formulation and actually implementing it in code. The blanks force students to think about: what to return when there is only 1 element (base case: return data[0]), and how to combine one element with the recursive result (return rsum(data, len-1) + data[len-1]).

title: Recursive Call Timeline for Array Sum
summary: Traces the complete execution of recursive array sum rsum(data,4), showing how each instance has its own len and sum variables, returning 30.
main_text: Each instance of rsum has its own len argument and sum variable. Every instance of a function has its own copy of local variables. The recursive sum function: int rsum(int data[], int len) { if(len == 1) return data[0]; else int sum = rsum(data, len-1); return sum + data[len-1]; }. Execution trace for data[4] = {8,6,7,9}: rsum(data,4): calls rsum(data,3), gets sum=21, returns 21+data[3]=21+9=30. rsum(data,3): calls rsum(data,2), gets sum=14, returns 14+data[2]=14+7=21. rsum(data,2): calls rsum(data,1), gets sum=8, returns 8+data[1]=8+6=14. rsum(data,1): base case, returns data[0]=8. The calls proceed in order 4,3,2,1 and returns propagate back 8,14,21,30.
notes_text: This timeline visualization is crucial for understanding how recursive calls unfold over time. The leftward arrows show the chain of recursive calls (going deeper), while the rightward arrows show the returns (coming back up). Each level is responsible for adding one element (data[len-1]) to the sum of all previous elements.

images.description: Timeline diagram showing four levels of recursive calls from rsum(data,4) down to rsum(data,1), with arrows showing call direction (right) and return values (left). Each level shows its len value and computed sum, with final result 30 propagating back.

title: Head Recursion for Array Sum
summary: Shows head recursion approach to array summing where recursion happens first, then summing occurs on the way back up through return values.
main_text: Recurse first and then start summing as we return from each recursion (on the way back up). Each function is responsible for the LAST element in the array. Code: int rsumh(int data[], int len) { if(len == 1) { return data[0]; } else { int s_in = rsumh(data, len-1); return s_in + data[len-1]; } }. Execution trace with box diagrams: Main() has dat=0x800. rsumh(dat,4) calls rsumh(dat,3) which calls rsumh(dat,2) which calls rsumh(dat,1). rsumh(dat,1) returns 8 (data[0]). rsumh(dat,2) returns 6+8=14. rsumh(dat,3) returns 7+14=21. rsumh(dat,4) returns 9+21=30. The red dashed arrow shows the return path carrying accumulated sums back to main.
notes_text: In head recursion, the function recurses all the way down to the base case first, then builds the solution on the way back up. Each function instance adds its responsible element (data[len-1]) to the sum returned by the recursive call. The data array pointer is the same across all calls (passed by pointer), but each call has its own len parameter.

images.description: Box diagram showing four instances of rsumh function connected by dashed arrows. Each box shows the array portion it sees and its computed result. Returns flow back: 8, 14(6+8), 21(7+14), 30(9+21).

title: Tail Recursion for Array Sum
summary: Shows tail recursion approach where the sum is accumulated as a parameter while walking down the array, returning the final answer from the deepest call.
main_text: Produce sum as you walk down the array then just return the final answer back up the array. Each function is responsible for the LAST element in the array. Code: int rsumt(int data[], int len, int s_in) { if(len == 0) { return s_in; } else { int s_out = s_in + data[len-1]; return rsumt(data, len-1, s_out); } }. Called from main as: int sumt = rsumt(data, 4, s_in=0). Execution trace: rsumt(dat,4,0) computes s_out=0+9=9, calls rsumt(dat,3,9). rsumt(dat,3,9) computes s_out=9+7=16, calls rsumt(dat,2,16). rsumt(dat,2,16) computes s_out=16+6=22, calls rsumt(dat,1,22). rsumt(dat,1,22) computes s_out=22+8=30, calls rsumt(dat,0,30). rsumt(dat,0,30) returns 30. All calls then return 30 back up.
notes_text: In tail recursion, the computation is done on the way DOWN rather than on the way back up. The running sum is passed as a parameter (s_in). By the time the base case is reached, the answer is already computed and just needs to be returned through all the call levels. This is more efficient because the compiler can potentially optimize tail recursive calls to avoid creating new stack frames (tail call optimization).

images.description: Box diagram showing five instances of rsumt with accumulated sum growing: 0->9->16->22->30. Red dashed arrows show all calls return the same final value 30 back up the chain.

title: Tail Recursion with Reference Parameter [1]
summary: Demonstrates using a reference parameter to collect all intermediate results during tail recursion, computing and storing all factorial values 1! through n!.
main_text: What if we didn't want to JUST compute n! but to compute AND store ALL the factorial values between 1! and n! in an array/vector? Often this is a better way: Have all recursions take in a REFERENCE argument so that all recursive calls see/share one object/variable that can collect their results. Code: void rsumt(int data[], int len, int& sum) { if(len == 0) { return s_in; } else { sum += data[len-1]; rsumt(data, len-1, sum); } }. The reference parameter sum is shared across all recursive calls. As each call adds data[len-1] to sum, the shared variable accumulates: 0->9->16->22->30. All function instances point to the same sum variable in main's stack frame.
notes_text: Using a reference parameter is a powerful technique that allows all levels of recursion to share a single variable. This is especially useful when you need to collect results from multiple recursive calls or accumulate state. The key insight is that unlike regular parameters which are copied for each call, reference parameters all point to the same memory location.

images.description: Box diagram showing all rsumt instances connected by arrows to a shared sum variable in Main's frame. The sum variable shows progressive values: 0, 9, 16, 22, 30. Blue arrows from each recursive instance point back to the shared sum.

title: Tail Recursion with Reference Parameter [2] - Factorial Vector
summary: Shows how to use a reference vector parameter to store all factorial values from 1! to n! during recursive computation.
main_text: What if we didn't want to JUST compute n! but to compute AND store ALL the factorial values between 1! and n! in an array/vector. Often this is a better way: Have all recursions take in a REFERENCE argument so that all recursive calls see/share one object/variable that can collect their results. Code: int fact(int n, vector<int> res) { if(n == 1) { res.push_back(1); return 1; } else { int ans = fact(n-1, res) * n; res.push_back(ans); return ans; } }. Execution trace for fact(4, results): fact(4,res) calls fact(3,res) calls fact(2,res) calls fact(1,res). fact(1,res): pushes 1, returns 1. fact(2,res): ans=1*2=2, pushes 2, returns 2. fact(3,res): ans=2*3=6, pushes 6, returns 6. fact(4,res): ans=6*4=24, pushes 24. Results vector contains [1, 2, 6, 24].
notes_text: This example shows a practical application of reference parameters in recursion: building up a collection of intermediate results. The vector res is passed by reference so all recursive calls add to the same vector. The results are added in order from smallest (1!) to largest (n!) because push_back happens on the way back up (head recursion pattern).

images.description: Box diagram showing four instances of fact function. Each box shows n value and ans value. The shared res vector accumulates values [1, 2, 6, 24]. Arrows show call and return flow with computed values.

title: Tail Recursion with Reference Parameter [3] - Complete Example
summary: Complete implementation of factorial with reference vector parameter, showing the results vector populated with [1, 2, 6, 24] for fact(4).
main_text: What if we didn't want to JUST compute n! but to compute AND store ALL the factorial values between 1! and n! in an array/vector. Often this is a better way: Have all recursions take in a REFERENCE argument so that all recursive calls see/share one object/variable that can collect their results. Complete code: int main() { vector<int> results; fact(4, results); // use results }. int fact(int n, vector<int>& res) { if(n == 1) { res.push_back(1); return 1; } else { int ans = fact(n-1, res) * n; res.push_back(ans); return ans; } }. The results vector is passed by reference (vector<int>& res). After execution, the results vector in main contains [1, 2, 6, 24].
notes_text: Note the ampersand (&) in the parameter declaration: vector<int>& res. This is what makes res a reference parameter, meaning all recursive calls modify the same vector object. Without the ampersand, each call would get its own copy and the results would be lost when each call returns.

images.description: Box diagram showing Main() with results vector [1, 2, 6, 24], and four fact function instances connected by arrows. Each instance shows n and ans values, with dashed lines to the shared results vector.

title: Recursion Double Check [1] - Base Cases
summary: First verification step for recursive functions: check that you have appropriate base cases and check for them first, with examples of correct and incorrect code.
main_text: When you write a recursive routine: Check that you have appropriate base cases. Need to check for these first before recursive cases. Two code examples shown side by side. Correct example (Fibonacci): int fib(int n) { if(n == 1) { return 1; } else { return fib(n-1)+fib(n-2); } }. This correctly checks the base case first. Incorrect example (Factorial): int fact(int n) { int ans = n * fact(n-1); if(n == 1) { ans = 1; // TOO LATE } return ans; }. In the incorrect version, the recursive call fact(n-1) is made BEFORE checking if n == 1, so the base case check comes too late. The function will recurse infinitely because it never stops before making the next call.
notes_text: This is the first of three critical double-checks for recursive functions. The order matters: the base case must be checked BEFORE making any recursive calls. In the incorrect example, even though there is a base case check (n == 1), it happens after the recursive call has already been made, making it useless. This is a common beginner mistake.

title: Recursion Double Check [2] - Progress Toward Base Case
summary: Second verification step: ensure each recursive call makes progress toward the base case, otherwise you get infinite recursion and stack overflow.
main_text: When you write a recursive routine: Check that each recursive call makes progress toward the base case. Otherwise, you'll get an infinite loop and stack overflow. Incorrect example: int fact(int n) { if(n == 1) { return 1; } return n * fact(n); // NO PROGRESS }. In this code, fact(n) calls fact(n) instead of fact(n-1). Since n never decreases, the function never gets closer to the base case of n == 1. This results in infinite recursion, where each call adds a new frame to the stack until the stack memory is exhausted, causing a stack overflow error.
notes_text: This is the second critical check. The recursive call must pass a 'smaller' version of the problem. For numeric parameters, this usually means decrementing (n-1) or dividing (n/2). For arrays, it means reducing the length. For linked lists, it means advancing to the next node. The 'NO PROGRESS' comment highlights the bug: fact(n) instead of fact(n-1).

title: Recursion Double Check [3] - Return Statement at Each Level
summary: Third verification step: ensure every recursive level has a return statement to pass values back through the call chain.
main_text: When you write a recursive routine: Check that you use a return statement at EACH level to return appropriate values back to each recursive call. You have to return through EVERY level of recursion, so make sure each one returns something (the appropriate thing). Incorrect example: int fact(int n) { if(n == 1) { return 1; } n * fact(n-1); // NO RETURN }. In this code, the recursive case computes n * fact(n-1) but does not return the result. The box diagram shows fact(1) correctly returns 1, fact(2) computes 1*2=2 but the return value is lost (?? shown), fact(3) computes ??*3=6 but again ?? is returned, and fact(4) computes 4*??=24 but ?? propagates. Without proper return statements, the computed values are discarded and undefined values propagate back.
notes_text: This is a very common mistake, especially for beginners. In C/C++, forgetting to write 'return' before an expression means the value is computed but thrown away, and the function returns an undefined/garbage value. The box diagram clearly shows the ?? values propagating through the call chain, producing incorrect results even though the computation itself is correct.

images.description: Box diagram showing four fact function instances. fact(1) returns 1 correctly, but fact(2), fact(3), and fact(4) show ?? for their return values because the return keyword is missing. The computed values (2, 6, 24) are shown but marked with ?? indicating they are not properly returned.

title: Recursion Double Check Summary
summary: Summarizes all three verification checks for recursive functions: appropriate base cases, progress toward base case, and return statements at each level.
main_text: When you write a recursive routine, perform these three checks: 1. Check that you have appropriate base cases. Need to check for these first before recursive cases. 2. Check that each recursive call makes progress toward the base case. Otherwise, you'll get an infinite loop and stack overflow. 3. Check that you use a return statement at EACH level to return appropriate values back to each recursive call. You have to return back up through EVERY level of recursion, so make sure you are returning something (the appropriate thing).
notes_text: These three checks form a comprehensive verification checklist that should be applied every time you write a recursive function. Missing any one of these will cause the function to fail: missing base case leads to infinite recursion, no progress leads to infinite recursion, and missing returns leads to incorrect results. Use this checklist as a debugging tool when recursive functions produce unexpected behavior.

title: More Examples: Binary Search and Sorting Algorithms
summary: Section divider introducing the next set of topics: recursive binary search and sorting algorithms.
main_text: This section transitions to more advanced examples of recursion applied to binary search and sorting algorithms. These are practical applications that demonstrate how recursion naturally fits certain algorithmic patterns, particularly divide-and-conquer strategies.
notes_text: Binary search and sorting are classic examples where recursion provides elegant solutions. Binary search naturally decomposes into searching a smaller half of the array. Some sorting algorithms (like merge sort and quicksort) are inherently recursive divide-and-conquer algorithms.

title: Recursive Binary Search
summary: Explains recursive binary search on a sorted array using start/end indices, with base case for empty range and three comparison outcomes.
main_text: Perform a binary search for target in a sorted array. Assume remaining items = [start, end). start is the inclusive index of start item in remaining list. end is the exclusive index of end item (1 beyond the end) in remaining list. Put another way, consider items at index i such that: start <= i < end. binSearch(target, list[], start, end): Perform base check (empty range/list) - Return NOT FOUND (-1). Pick mid item. Based on comparison of target with list[mid]: EQ (equal) => Found => return mid. LT (less than) => return answer to binSearch[start, mid). GT (greater than) => return answer to binSearch[mid+1, end). Example searching for target=11 in list [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19]: First call: start=0, mid=4, end=9. Since 11 > list[4]=9, search right half. Second call: start=5, mid=6, end=9. Since 11 < list[6]=13, search left half. Third call: start=5, end=6, mid=5. list[5]=11, found! Return 5.
notes_text: Recursive binary search is a natural fit for recursion because the problem naturally decomposes: each step eliminates half the search space. The use of [start, end) half-open intervals is a common convention that simplifies the base case check (start >= end means empty). The three cases (equal, less than, greater than) correspond to finding the target, recursing left, or recursing right.

images.description: Step-by-step visualization of binary search for target=11 in array [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19]. Three stages shown with array, indices, and start/mid/end markers narrowing down to the target location at index 5.

title: Sorting with Bubble/Selection Sort
summary: Introduces sorting algorithms and demonstrates bubble/selection sort which finds the maximum and places it at the end, then repeats on a smaller list.
main_text: If we have an unordered list, sequential search becomes our only choice. If we will perform a lot of searches it may be beneficial to sort the list, then use binary search. Many sorting algorithms of differing complexity (i.e. faster or slower). Bubble or Selection Sort: Simple though not terribly efficient. On each pass through the list, pick up the maximum element and place it at the end of the list. Then repeat using a list of size n-1 (i.e. without the newly placed maximum value). Example sorting [7,3,8,6,5,1]: After Pass 1: [3,7,6,5,1,8] - 8 placed at end. After Pass 2: [3,6,5,1,7,8] - 7 placed at end. After Pass 3: [3,5,1,6,7,8] - 6 placed. After Pass 4: [3,1,5,6,7,8] - 5 placed. After Pass 5: [1,3,5,6,7,8] - sorted. This naturally maps to recursion: sort(n) places max at end, then calls sort(n-1).
notes_text: Bubble/selection sort has O(n^2) time complexity, making it inefficient for large datasets. However, its simplicity makes it a good teaching example. The recursive nature is clear: after placing the largest element, the remaining problem is sorting a list of size n-1, which is a smaller version of the same problem. The base case is a list of size 1 (already sorted).

images.description: Step-by-step visualization of selection sort on array [7,3,8,6,5,1] showing 5 passes. After each pass, the largest unsorted element (highlighted in red) is placed at the end of the unsorted portion. Final result: [1,3,5,6,7,8].

title: Multiple Recursive Calls
summary: Section divider introducing the concept of functions that make more than one recursive call per invocation.
main_text: This section covers multiple recursive calls, where a single function invocation makes two or more recursive calls. This pattern appears in algorithms like Fibonacci, merge sort, tree traversals, and other divide-and-conquer approaches. Multiple recursive calls create a tree-like execution pattern rather than the linear chain seen in single-call recursion.
notes_text: Multiple recursive calls are where recursion truly shines over iteration. While single recursive calls can always be easily replaced with a loop, multiple recursive calls create branching execution patterns that are much harder to express iteratively. This is the key reason recursion is preferred for tree-like and divide-and-conquer problems.

title: When to Use Loops vs. Recursion
summary: Provides guidelines for choosing between loops and recursion: use a loop for single recursive calls, use recursion for multiple recursive calls.
main_text: ANY problem that can be solved using recursion can also be solved with iteration and other appropriate data structures. Guideline: Each recursion calls itself ONCE? Use a loop! Each recursion calls itself MORE THAN ONCE? Use recursion! Why use recursion? Usually clean and elegant solutions to problems that would be VERY difficult to solve with loops. (Usually, when each recursion calls itself more than once.) Can lead to stack overflow if recursive depth is too large. Is one 'more efficient'? Iteration is usually faster and uses less memory and should be used when possible. However, if iteration produces a very complex solution, consider recursion. Code examples: void rfunc1(int n) { ... rfunc1(n-1); ... } - calls itself once, use a loop instead. void rfunc2(int n) { ... t = rfunc2(n-1); s = rfunc2(n-2); ... } - calls itself twice, use recursion.
notes_text: This is a crucial practical guideline. Single recursive calls create a linear chain that maps directly to a loop. Multiple recursive calls create a tree of calls that is exponentially harder to express iteratively (requiring explicit stack data structures). The efficiency note is important: recursion has overhead from function calls and stack frame creation, so iteration is preferred when the solution is equally simple.

title: Flood Fill Exercise
summary: Exercise slide directing students to complete a Codio recursion exercise on flood fill.
main_text: Codio Recursion Exercise on Flood Fill. Students are directed to complete an interactive coding exercise implementing the flood fill algorithm recursively.
notes_text: Flood fill is an excellent example of multiple recursive calls since each pixel can recursively fill its neighbors in up to 4 directions (up, down, left, right). This creates a branching recursive pattern that would be complex to implement iteratively.

title: Flood Fill Algorithm
summary: Explains the flood fill algorithm for shading shapes in an image using recursion with base cases for black pixels and out-of-bounds.
main_text: Imagine you are given an image with outlines of shapes (boxes and circles) and you had to write a program to shade (make black) the inside of one of the shapes. How would you do it? Flood fill is a recursive approach. Given a pixel: Base case: If it is black already, stop! Recursive case: Call floodfill on each neighbor pixel. Hidden base case: If pixel out of bounds, stop! The algorithm starts at a point inside a shape and recursively colors each neighboring pixel, spreading outward until it hits boundaries (already-black pixels or image edges). The slide shows before/after images of shapes being filled.
notes_text: Flood fill is used in paint programs (the 'bucket fill' tool) and in game algorithms. It is a prime example of multiple recursive calls (4 directions: up, down, left, right) creating a branching execution. The 'hidden base case' of boundary checking is important and often forgotten, leading to array index out-of-bounds errors. This algorithm naturally requires recursion because the fill pattern is unpredictable and depends on the shape's geometry.

images.description: Before and after images showing shapes (rectangle and circle) as outlines that get filled in with solid black after flood fill is applied. The outline shapes are on top, and the filled versions are on the bottom.

title: Exercise: Ruler
summary: Exercise slide directing students to practice a recursive ruler drawing exercise.
main_text: Exercises: Ruler. Students are asked to implement a recursive ruler drawing exercise. A ruler pattern involves drawing tick marks of varying heights at different positions, which naturally decomposes recursively: draw the middle tick, then recursively draw the left half and right half of the ruler.
notes_text: The ruler exercise is another example of multiple recursive calls (two calls per invocation for left and right halves). It demonstrates how recursion can generate fractal-like patterns that would be complex to produce iteratively.

title: Linked Lists and Data Structures
summary: Section divider introducing recursion applied to linked lists and other data structures.
main_text: This section covers how recursion applies to linked lists and data structures. Linked lists have an inherently recursive structure: each node points to the next node, forming a chain where each sub-list starting from any node looks just like the full list. This self-similar structure makes linked lists natural candidates for recursive processing.
notes_text: The recursive nature of linked lists is a key insight. A linked list is either empty (base case) or a node followed by another linked list (recursive case). This structural recursion is different from the numeric recursion seen in factorial, but the same principles of base case and recursive case apply.

title: Recursion and Linked Lists
summary: Shows how a linked list node's next pointer acts as a head pointer to the remaining list, enabling recursive processing by passing next as the new head.
main_text: Notice that one Item's next pointer looks like a head pointer to the remainder of the linked list. If we have a function that processes a linked list by receiving the head pointer as a parameter, we can recursively call that function by passing our 'next' pointer as the 'head'. The 'next' pointer of an Item struct can act as a 'head' pointer to the remaining list. Example linked list: head (0x148) -> Node{val:3, next:0x1c0} -> Node{val:9, next:0x168} -> Node{val:2, next:0x0 (Null)}. From the perspective of the second node, its next pointer (0x168) is a head pointer to a sub-list containing just node {val:2}. This structural property makes linked lists naturally recursive.
notes_text: This is a key conceptual insight. The recursive structure of linked lists mirrors the recursive structure of the algorithms that process them. Each node sees itself as the 'head' of a smaller list. The base case is when the next pointer is NULL (end of list). This pattern extends to trees, where each node has two 'next' pointers (left and right children), each serving as the root of a subtree.

images.description: Linked list diagram showing head pointer (0x148) pointing to three nodes connected by next pointers. Node 1: val=3, next=0x1c0. Node 2: val=9, next=0x168. Node 3: val=2, next=0x0 (Null). A circle highlights how the head pointer connects to the first node, and the next pointer of each node acts similarly.

title: Guiding Principle for Recursive Solutions
summary: Summarizes the guiding principle: recursive code should handle only 1 element (array element, linked list node, tree node, or choice), then recurse on remaining.
main_text: A useful principle when trying to develop recursive solutions is that the recursive code should handle only 1 element, which might be: 1. An element in an array. 2. A node in a linked list. 3. A node in a tree. 4. One choice in a sequence of choices. Then use recursion to handle the remaining elements. And finally combine the solution(s) from the recursive call(s) with the one element being handled. Three visual examples shown: (1) Array: f(n) handles element at index 0, f(n-1) handles the rest. (2) Linked list: f(head) handles the first node, f(head->next) handles the rest. (3) Tree: each node handles itself, f(left) handles the left subtree, f(right) handles the right subtree.
notes_text: This principle unifies all the recursive patterns covered in this unit. Whether dealing with arrays, linked lists, trees, or abstract choices, the same decomposition strategy applies: handle one piece, recurse on the rest, combine. For trees, this naturally involves multiple recursive calls (left and right subtrees), which is why tree algorithms are almost always recursive.

images.description: Three diagrams illustrating the guiding principle: (1) Array with f(n) box around first element and f(n-1) around the rest. (2) Linked list with f(head) on first node and f(head->next) on remaining nodes (3,9,7). (3) Tree with root node calling f(left) and f(right) on its subtrees.

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions to previous exercises.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the solutions section, which provides answers to the exercises presented earlier in the lecture.
notes_text: Solutions section for the exercises including count-down, count-up, and other recursive problems from the lecture.

title: Head vs. Tail Recursion Solution
summary: Solution slide showing completed execution traces for both tail recursion (Go, Go, Stop) and head recursion (Stop, Go, Go) versions of doit(3).
main_text: Tail Recursion: Some work is performed and then the recursive call is made. Head Recursion: Recursive call is made before the real work is performed in the function body. Tail Recursion solution for doit(3): doit(3) prints 'Go', then calls doit(2). doit(2) prints 'Go', then calls doit(1). doit(1) prints 'Stop'. Output: Go, Go, Stop. Head Recursion solution for doit(3): doit(3) calls doit(2) immediately. doit(2) calls doit(1) immediately. doit(1) prints 'Stop'. Then doit(2) returns and prints 'Go'. Then doit(3) returns and prints 'Go'. Output: Stop, Go, Go. The tail recursion produces output in forward order (top-down), while head recursion produces output in reverse order (bottom-up).
notes_text: This solution confirms that the placement of work relative to the recursive call determines the output order. Tail recursion processes from the first call to the last (forward), while head recursion processes from the last call to the first (reverse). Understanding this is essential for predicting recursive function behavior.

images.description: Two side-by-side execution traces with box diagrams showing the call and return flow for tail recursion (left, output: Go, Go, Stop) and head recursion (right, output: Stop, Go, Go)

title: Unused Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking unused/supplementary slides.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of unused or supplementary material that was not covered in the main lecture.
notes_text: Supplementary slides that may be used for additional reference or in future iterations of the course.

title: Recursive Call Timeline - Factorial with small_ans
summary: Alternative presentation of factorial recursive call timeline using small_ans variable to store the recursive result before multiplying.
main_text: Value/version of n is implicitly 'saved' and 'restored' as we move from one instance of the 'fact' function to the next. Code: int fact(int n) { if(n == 1) { return 1; } else { int small_ans = fact(n-1); return n * small_ans; } }. Timeline for Fact(3): Fact(3) with n=3 calls Fact(2). Fact(2) with n=2 calls Fact(1). Fact(1) with n=1 returns 1 (base case). Fact(2) receives small_ans=1, returns n*small_ans = 2*1 = 2. Fact(3) receives small_ans=2, returns n*small_ans = 3*2 = 6. The variable name 'small_ans' emphasizes that the recursive call returns the answer to a smaller version of the problem.
notes_text: Using the variable name 'small_ans' is a pedagogical technique that reinforces the concept that the recursive call solves a smaller version of the same problem. This naming convention makes it explicit that you are receiving the solution to a sub-problem and then combining it with your current element to produce the solution to the larger problem.

images.description: Timeline diagram showing three boxes for Fact(3), Fact(2), and Fact(1) connected by arrows. Each box shows n value and small_ans computation. Arrows indicate call direction (right) and return flow (left) with computed values.

title: System Stack and Recursion
summary: Shows how the system stack provides separate memory for each recursive call instance, with a complete stack diagram for rsum_it(data, 4).
main_text: The system stack makes recursion possible by providing separate memory storage for the local variables of each running instance of the function. Code: int main() { int data[4] = {8, 6, 7, 9}; int sum2 = rsum_it(data, 4); }. int rsum_it(int data[], int len) { if(len == 1) return data[0]; else int sum = rsum_it(data, len-1); return sum + data[len-1]; }. The System Stack Area shows the stack frames: At the bottom is main's frame (data=800, sum2=??). Above it: rsum_it(data=800, len=4, sum=21). Then rsum_it(data=800, len=3, sum=14). Then rsum_it(data=800, len=2, sum=8). At top: rsum_it(data=800, len=1, sum=??). Each frame has its own return link. The data array at address 800 contains {8,6,7,9}.
notes_text: This slide provides the low-level memory view of how recursion works. The system stack (also called the call stack) grows upward with each recursive call. Each stack frame contains the function's local variables, parameters, and a return link. When a function returns, its stack frame is deallocated. This is why too-deep recursion causes stack overflow: the stack runs out of memory.

images.description: Diagram showing the system stack area in RAM with five colored stack frames stacked vertically. Bottom frame is main's data, followed by four rsum_it frames with increasing len values. Each frame shows data pointer, len, sum, and return link. The data array {8,6,7,9} is shown separately at address 800.

title: Old/Unused - Missing Return Box Diagram
summary: Supplementary slide showing box diagram for factorial with missing return statement, demonstrating undefined behavior with ?? values.
main_text: This is an old/unused supplementary slide showing a box diagram for the missing return statement bug in factorial. The box diagram shows: Main() calls fact(4). fact(4): n=4, ans=6, computes 4*??=24, result is 4*6=24. fact(3): n=3, ans=2, computes ??*3=6, result is ??. fact(2): n=2, ans=1, computes 1*2=2, result is ??. fact(1): n=1, returns 1. The ?? values indicate that without a return statement in the recursive case, the computed values are not properly passed back. While the local computations may be correct, the values returned to the calling function are undefined.
notes_text: This supplementary slide reinforces the importance of return statements at every level of recursion. The box diagram format makes the propagation of undefined values visually clear.

images.description: Box diagram showing four fact function instances with n and ans values. fact(1) returns 1 correctly but subsequent levels show ?? for returned values despite correct local computations, illustrating the missing return statement bug.
